strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel and practically relevant failure mode, Marginal Path Collapse, in heterogeneous diffusion steering, with a clear theoretical criterion (PEC) that characterizes when the composed intermediate density is normalizable.

Provides a rigorous theoretical framework: Theorem 2.1 (and Theorem B.1) proves sufficiency and necessity of the PEC for Gaussian-to-compactly-supported targets, with extensions to Gaussian mixtures (Theorem B.3) and a constructive adaptive exponent correction (Theorem 2.2) that guarantees path existence while preserving endpoint exponents.

Generalizes Feynman-Kac steering to time-varying exponents (Theorem 2.3/ A.1), yielding a practical algorithm (ACE) with importance weights and resampling; the derivation is sound and includes auxiliary dynamics for tracking component log-densities.

Offers a valuable theoretical insight linking the PEC to concentration control (Proposition 2.1/ E.1), explaining why ACE stabilizes sampling even when the path already exists, and supporting the observed gains in homogeneous settings.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple domains: synthetic 2D checkerboard, flexible-pose scaffold decoration with heterogeneous DN/CONF/SBDD experts, fragment linking, and COCO-MIG compositional image generation, consistently showing improvements over NR, FKC, and task-specific baselines.

Demonstrates strong practical impact in drug design: ACE achieves significantly higher optimization success rates and better Vina scores than specialized fixed-pose baselines (Delete, AutoFragDiff) and constant-exponent correctors, with a practical ACE-lite variant that reduces runtime overhead.

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analyses (bump parameters, ESS threshold, time-varying heuristic schedules, schedule alignment) and a prevalence study showing that collapse occurs in 41–80% of heterogeneous schedule combinations, supporting the claim that this is not an edge case.
Includes an honest limitations section and an ethics impact statement discussing dual-use risks in generative chemistry.
weaknesses: Reproducibility gap: the reproducibility statement says "we have provided the complete source code ... at" but no URL or supplementary link is given in the manuscript, which hinders independent verification.

Some experiments lack statistical rigor: fragment linking uses a single random seed, COCO-MIG results report no error bars or significance tests, and scaffold decoration OSR values lack variance estimates, making it difficult to assess the reliability of the reported gains.

Theoretical scope is limited to Gaussian-to-compactly-supported targets and Gaussian mixtures; non-compact, heavy-tailed targets and latent diffusion models are not covered, which restricts applicability to many modern generative models.

Comparison with fixed-pose scaffold decoration baselines (Delete, AutoFragDiff) may not be entirely fair, as ACE operates in a more flexible pose setting that explores a larger search space; while the authors argue this is a strength, the task definitions differ.

Presentation issues: inconsistent notation (e.g., α_i^{(i)} instead of α_t^{(i)} in Section 2.1), a confusing table label in Table 2 ("ACE(B1=1.5)" with a B1 column), and a dense main text with many forward references to appendices that can make the core contributions harder to follow.

The ACE sampler requires estimating divergences of expert score/velocity fields (e.g., via Hutchinson's estimator), which can introduce high variance and may limit scalability to very large models; runtime is approximately 1.8× that of FKC/NR in the molecular experiments.

The truncation at t_end < 1 and the one-step Euler jump to t=1 is justified only heuristically (O((1-t_end)^2) error claimed negligible), without rigorous error quantification for high-dimensional or stiff SDEs.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underappreciated failure mode, Marginal Path Collapse, in heterogeneous ratio-of-densities diffusion steering, and provides a clear 2D demonstration.
The Path Existence Criterion (Theorem 2.1/B.1) is a clean, tractable sufficient and necessary condition for compactly supported targets, with a rigorous proof based on Gaussian envelope bounds.
ACE generalizes Feynman-Kac steering to time-varying exponents and provides a constructive bump-function protocol that provably ensures C(t)>0 up to t_end (Theorem 2.2/B.2).
The synthetic checkerboard experiments show substantial improvements over NR and FKC when schedules are heterogeneous, supporting the theory in a controlled setting.
The work targets an important application area (AI for science, structure-based drug design) and reports large gains in OSR on scaffold decoration, suggesting practical potential.
Limitations and scope (compact support, linear scaling, misaligned experts) are discussed in a dedicated section.
weaknesses: The molecular application is not soundly implemented: the Bayesian decomposition requires the marginal p(M^sc) under the prior, but the paper uses the same joint DN model for both p(M) and p(M^sc). A joint diffusion model does not provide the marginal density; evaluating its score on scaffold coordinates is not the score of the marginal. Thus the claimed target distribution is not actually sampled.

The truncation at t_end and single Euler jump to t=1 is not justified. The bump is positive at t_end, so the corrected path at t_end does not match the original target, and the final jump ignores the rapid exponent change; the O((1-t_end)^2) error claim is insufficient.
Proposition 2.1/E.1 assumes a uniform lower bound Z_t >= m_* without proof, which is a significant gap for the claimed concentration control.
Algorithm 1's weight update uses \hat{\gamma}_i(t) instead of \dot{\gamma}_i(t), contradicting Theorem A.1. If implemented as written, the sampler is incorrect; this harms reproducibility.

Experimental validation is limited: only one molecular task with 76 pockets and 5 samples per pocket, no error bars for OSR; fragment linking uses a single seed; the image experiment is homogeneous and does not ablate the bump choice.
The paper overclaims 'provably ensures path existence' and 'guarantees a valid path from noise to data' given the truncation and restricted compact-support assumption.
Presentation is dense and contains notation inconsistencies (e.g., alpha/beta labels in Table C.1, q_i^{(i)} typo), and the reproducibility statement lacks a concrete code URL.
The criterion is restricted to compactly supported targets; applicability to general unbounded diffusion models is not established.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes Marginal Path Collapse, a real and important failure mode in ratio-of-densities diffusion steering with heterogeneous experts, negative exponents, or mismatched schedules.
Provides a tractable and sharp Path Existence Criterion under Gaussian-to-compactly-supported interpolants, with sufficiency and necessity proofs and a separate treatment of the C(t)=0 boundary case.

Generalizes Feynman-Kac steering to time-varying exponents (ACE) with a constructive bump-function protocol that preserves endpoint exponents while enforcing C(t)>0, plus weighted SDE/ODE sampling dynamics and practical algorithms.
Links path validity to stability through a quantile-radius bound scaling as 1/sqrt(C(t)), giving theoretical motivation for why ACE stabilizes intermediate distributions even when collapse is absent.

Empirically validates ACE on synthetic checkerboard composition, flexible-pose scaffold decoration with DN/CONF/SBDD experts, fragment linking, and COCO-MIG image composition, showing consistent gains over NR/FKC and competitive results against specialized baselines.
Includes extensive appendices with schedule definitions, hyperparameters, dataset details, and an explicit limitations/ethics discussion, including dual-use considerations for generative chemistry.
weaknesses: The core Path Existence Criterion relies on compactly supported targets and Gaussian-to-compactly-supported stochastic interpolants; many practical diffusion models, especially latent diffusion and molecular models with effectively unbounded support, fall outside this assumption, so the guarantee is not fully general.

The guarantee covers only [0,t_end] with t_end<1; the final transition to t=1 uses an Euler jump over the potentially collapsed region (t_end,1), making exact target recovery an approximation rather than a proven consequence of the theory.
The Reproducibility Statement references code availability but the provided manuscript lacks an actual URL, and some experimental details (e.g., seeds) are only said to be in configuration files.

Presentation issues remain: notation is dense, main-text Table 2 has confusing/inconsistent B1/B2 labeling, and the algorithmic distinction between ACE-lite, ACE, FKC, and NR is not fully clear (e.g., why ACE-lite matches FKC runtime if it still tracks log q).

The molecular evaluations lack error bars or significance tests in the main tables and use a modest test set (76 pockets, 5 samples each); comparisons against fixed-pose specialized baselines involve different task assumptions, so the 'outperforms specialized baselines' claim is not strictly apples-to-apples.

The homogeneous image-generation gains are demonstrated on one backbone with a single small bump value and no direct measurement of the proposed quantile-radius mechanism, leaving the empirical link to the theory somewhat indirect.
